title: Ensemble Methods and Model Evaluation
summary: This lesson teaches how ensemble methods—random forests and gradient boosting—combine many weak learners into strong predictive models, and how to rigorously evaluate them using cross-validation and metrics like ROC-AUC. You will learn the bias-variance intuition behind bagging and boosting, key hyperparameters, and a practical workflow to optimize a classifier.
objectives: Explain the difference between bagging (random forests) and boosting (gradient boosting) and when to use each.
Train random forest and gradient boosting classifiers in scikit-learn with sensible hyperparameters.
Use k-fold and stratified cross-validation to obtain reliable performance estimates.
Select and interpret evaluation metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC.
Tune hyperparameters with grid/randomized search to optimize a model without overfitting.
Interpret feature importance to understand model behavior.

quiz.q: What is the primary effect of bagging (as in random forests)?
options: Reduces bias by focusing on errors sequentially
Reduces variance by averaging decorrelated models
Increases interpretability of a single tree
quiz.why: Bagging trains many models on bootstrap samples and averages them, which mainly reduces variance. Boosting is the one that reduces bias sequentially.

quiz.q: In gradient boosting, what does a lower learning_rate generally require?
options: More trees (n_estimators) to reach good performance
quiz.why: A smaller learning rate shrinks each tree's contribution, so you typically need more boosting rounds, but it often generalizes better.

quiz.q: Why use StratifiedKFold instead of plain KFold for classification?
options: It preserves class proportions in each fold
It removes the need for a test set
quiz.why: Stratified folds keep the class distribution consistent across folds, giving more reliable estimates, especially with imbalanced data.

quiz.q: Which metric is threshold-independent and measures ranking quality?
quiz.why: ROC-AUC measures the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative, independent of any decision threshold.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why can accuracy be misleading on imbalanced datasets?
quiz.answer: Because a model can achieve high accuracy by always predicting the majority class while completely failing to identify the rare positive cases.
quiz.why: With class imbalance, the majority class dominates accuracy, so metrics like precision, recall, F1, or PR-AUC give a truer picture.

quiz.q: Name the key reason you should not tune hyperparameters on your final test set.
quiz.answer: Tuning on the test set leaks information and produces an optimistic, biased performance estimate that won't generalize.
quiz.why: The test set must remain untouched to give an unbiased estimate; tuning on it causes overfitting to that set.

body_markdown:
## Why Ensembles?

A single decision tree is easy to interpret but tends to overfit (high variance) or underfit (high bias). **Ensemble methods** combine many models so that their errors partially cancel out, producing predictions that are more accurate and robust than any individual model.

Two dominant families exist:

- **Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating):** Train many models in parallel on bootstrap samples and average their predictions. This mainly reduces **variance**. Random forests are the classic example.
- **Boosting:** Train models sequentially, where each new model focuses on the errors of the previous ones. This mainly reduces **bias**. Gradient boosting (and XGBoost/LightGBM) are the leading examples.

## Random Forests

A random forest builds many decision trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the data, and at each split considers only a random subset of features. This **decorrelates** the trees so averaging them yields a large variance reduction.

Key hyperparameters:

- `n_estimators`: number of trees (more is usually better but slower; diminishing returns).
- `max_depth`: limits tree depth to control overfitting.
- `max_features`: number of features considered per split (e.g. `sqrt` for classification).
- `min_samples_leaf`: minimum samples per leaf, a smoothing/regularization knob.

Random forests are robust, need little tuning, handle mixed feature types, and provide feature importances out of the box.

## Gradient Boosting

Gradient boosting fits trees sequentially. Each tree is trained on the **residual errors** (gradients of the loss) of the current ensemble, gradually improving the fit. Because it minimizes bias aggressively, it can overfit if not regularized.

Key hyperparameters:

- `learning_rate`: shrinks each tree's contribution; lower values need more trees but generalize better.
- `n_estimators`: number of boosting rounds.
- `max_depth`: usually small (3-6) for boosting (weak learners).
- `subsample`: fraction of rows sampled per tree (stochastic gradient boosting).

Libraries like **XGBoost**, **LightGBM**, and **CatBoost** are fast, regularized implementations widely used in production and competitions.

## Cross-Validation

A single train/test split gives a noisy performance estimate. **k-fold cross-validation** splits data into k folds, trains on k-1 and validates on the remaining fold, rotating k times and averaging the scores. For classification, use **StratifiedKFold** to preserve class proportions in each fold.

Cross-validation is also the basis for hyperparameter search: never tune on your final test set. Use a nested or held-out test set for the final unbiased estimate.

## Evaluation Metrics

Choose metrics that match the business goal, especially with imbalanced classes:

- **Accuracy:** fraction correct; misleading when classes are imbalanced.
- **Precision:** of predicted positives, how many are truly positive (TP / (TP+FP)).
- **Recall (sensitivity):** of actual positives, how many were caught (TP / (TP+FN)).
- **F1:** harmonic mean of precision and recall.
- **ROC-AUC:** area under the ROC curve; probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. Threshold-independent and great for ranking quality.
- **PR-AUC:** more informative than ROC-AUC under severe class imbalance.

## Practical Workflow

1. Establish a baseline (e.g. a single tree or logistic regression).
2. Train a random forest and a gradient boosting model.
3. Evaluate with stratified cross-validation using ROC-AUC plus precision/recall.
4. Tune hyperparameters with `RandomizedSearchCV` (faster than full grid).
5. Inspect feature importances for sanity and insight.
6. Report final performance on a held-out test set.

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_features='sqrt', random_state=42)
rf_auc = cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='roc_auc')
print('RF ROC-AUC:', rf_auc.mean())

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=42)
gb_auc = cross_val_score(gb, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='roc_auc')
print('GB ROC-AUC:', gb_auc.mean())
```

## Key Takeaways

- Bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias.
- Random forests are robust defaults; gradient boosting often wins accuracy with careful tuning.
- Always validate with cross-validation and pick metrics suited to your problem and class balance.

slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll explore ensemble methods—random forests and gradient boosting—and learn how to evaluate them properly using cross-validation and metrics like ROC-AUC. By the end you'll have a practical workflow for optimizing a predictive model.

slides.title: Why Ensembles?
bullets: A single tree overfits (high variance) or underfits (high bias)
Ensembles combine many models so errors cancel out
Bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias
More accurate and robust than individual models
slides.narration: A single decision tree is easy to understand but unstable—it tends to overfit. Ensemble methods combine many models so their individual errors partially cancel, yielding stronger, more robust predictions. Two big families exist: bagging, which reduces variance, and boosting, which reduces bias.

slides.title: Random Forests (Bagging)
bullets: Many trees trained on bootstrap samples in parallel
Random feature subset per split decorrelates trees
Averaging predictions reduces variance
Robust default, minimal tuning, free feature importances
slides.narration: Random forests build many trees, each on a bootstrap sample, and at each split only consider a random subset of features. This decorrelates the trees, so averaging them dramatically reduces variance. They're a robust default that needs little tuning and gives feature importances for free.

slides.title: Gradient Boosting
bullets: Trees trained sequentially on previous errors (gradients)
Aggressively reduces bias, can overfit if unregularized
Key knobs: learning_rate, n_estimators, max_depth
XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost are fast production choices
slides.narration: Gradient boosting fits trees one after another, each correcting the residual errors of the ensemble so far. It reduces bias aggressively, which means it can overfit without regularization. The learning rate and number of estimators trade off together. In practice, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost are the fast, regularized go-to implementations.

slides.title: Cross-Validation
bullets: A single split gives a noisy estimate
k-fold rotates train/validation across k folds
Use StratifiedKFold to preserve class balance
Tune on CV, never on the final test set
slides.narration: One train-test split is noisy. K-fold cross-validation splits data into k folds, trains on k minus one and validates on the rest, rotating and averaging. For classification, use stratified folds to keep class proportions consistent. Remember to tune hyperparameters using cross-validation and reserve a separate test set for your final, unbiased estimate.

slides.title: Choosing Metrics
bullets: Accuracy misleads under class imbalance
Precision: correctness of positive predictions
Recall: coverage of actual positives
ROC-AUC: threshold-independent ranking quality
PR-AUC better under severe imbalance
slides.narration: Pick metrics that match your goal. Accuracy is misleading when classes are imbalanced. Precision measures how trustworthy your positive predictions are, recall measures how many positives you catch, and F1 balances them. ROC-AUC captures ranking quality independent of threshold, while PR-AUC is more informative when positives are rare.

slides.title: Comparing Models with CV
bullets: Score both models with the same CV splits
Use scoring='roc_auc' for ranking quality
Average across folds, check the spread
Higher mean and lower variance is better
slides.narration: To compare fairly, score both the random forest and gradient boosting model on the same cross-validation splits using ROC-AUC. Look at the mean across folds and also the variance—a model with a slightly lower mean but much tighter spread may be the safer production choice.

slides.title: Tuning and Interpretation
bullets: RandomizedSearchCV is faster than full grid search
Tune learning_rate + n_estimators together
Inspect feature_importances_ for sanity
Report final score on held-out test set
slides.narration: Use randomized search to explore hyperparameters efficiently—it's usually faster than an exhaustive grid. For boosting, tune learning rate and number of estimators together. Always inspect feature importances as a sanity check, then report your final performance on a held-out test set you never touched during tuning.

slides.title: Practical Workflow Recap
bullets: Baseline → random forest → gradient boosting
Validate with stratified CV and ROC-AUC
Tune with randomized search
Confirm on held-out test set
slides.narration: To recap the workflow: start with a simple baseline, then train a random forest and a gradient boosting model. Validate using stratified cross-validation with metrics suited to your problem, tune hyperparameters with randomized search, and confirm your final result on a held-out test set. Bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias—choose and tune accordingly.
